groups.text: Picture your program as a page of code, and something that walks through it, one line at a time.
It keeps its notes on a stack: one frame per call in progress, with its local variables.
Step into a call, and a frame goes on top.
Return, and it comes off.
This walker is a thread.
The J V M starts this one, called main.
It runs inside a process, one running J V M, with memory of its own.
Every object you create with new lives in one part of it: the heap.
A second thread, a worker, walks the same code with its own stack.
Both call settle, and each one gets its own frame.
But both can reach the same Payment on the heap.
That is how threads share data with no copying, and how two of them can change one object at the same moment.
Main sets its local total to three.
Does the worker's total change?
No. A local lives on its own thread's stack.
Only the heap is shared.
A core of the C P U runs a thread, one thread at a time.
On one core, the operating system lets main run for a short slice, saves its registers, and switches to the worker.
That is a context switch, thousands of times a second.
Both are in progress, taking turns.
That is concurrency.
Two cores run both at the same instant.
That is parallelism.
So on four cores, is a busy job faster on eight threads than on four?
No. In the lesson's demo, four threads took one hundred twenty-one milliseconds, and eight took one hundred twenty-five.
Once every core is busy, extra threads only take turns.
Calling run on a thread is a plain method call.
Main steps into the task itself, on its own stack.
No new thread exists, nothing fails, and the job is just as slow.
With start, the J V M asks the operating system for a new thread, with a new stack.
That thread calls run, and main goes on at once.
The rule. Every thread has its own stack, they all share the heap, and only start makes a new thread.
Check yourself. You split a report into four slices, and call run on a new thread for each.
On four cores, how much faster is it?
Not faster. Main runs the four slices itself, one after another.
